messages.subject: ess for one chain
parts:
I forgot to work on it.  It came to my mind that when I print the fitted object in rstan
if I have n_chain = 1, it threw an error, I guess, due to some recent changes on 
the variance function in stan, which does not allow input of length 1. 
So I made a tiny change on the computing ess to just use the variance 
computed from one chain as the variance estimate for the parameter as we talked before. 

--

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
parts:
Andrew:

Just a heads up that this message is one to pay attention
to.

Your and Kenny's variogram-based estimator for ESS is
defined using (k-1) in the denominator, where k is the
number of chains. Thus we'd technically get infinite
variance estimates and thus zero ESS with a single chain.

So what Jiqiang did was just revert to the standard
estimate for a single chain instead of using the
variogram-based estimator.

The altnernative would be to not let users run Stan
with num chains = 1, which seems unduly restrictive.

I suppose a midway ground is to launch a warning to
scold the user into using three (?) or more chains.

More below on technical details of the implementation.

On 8/29/12 2:36 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I forgot to work on it. It came to my mind that when I print the fitted object in rstan
> if I have n_chain = 1, it threw an error, I guess, due to some recent changes on
> the variance function in stan, which does not allow input of length 1.
> So I made a tiny change on the computing ess to just use the variance
> computed from one chain as the variance estimate for the parameter as we talked before.

Perfect.

Yes, I went back in and added some error checking to our
variance() function, which uses (n-1) in the denominator,
so isn't well-defined at n=1.

We could also add a second variance function that divides
by n. I don't know how we'd call them, maybe variance()
and variance_mle()?

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
parts:
On 8/29/12 5:22 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> One approach is to use the split chains we're already using for split R-hat.
> Then we have k at least 2 for sure.

I think we followed the BDA draft for ESS, which
does NOT split the chains. That is, it uses
unsplit var+ estimate and then whole chains
for autocovariance.

I really don't care at all how we do this,
though there's a simplicity and doc advantage
to having a single unified definition.

> In any case, we only want to report a single variance function, whatever it is we decide to do.
> Others can always do their own post-processing if they really want.

Which "report" are you talking about? I'm talking
about which functions are defined for use in the
Stan modeling language and which functions we define
in C++. Right now, we have a function variance()
that divides by (N-1) and we do not have a function
that divides by N.

There's no way for a user to correct the unbiased
variance to the MLE in the case of one sample
after our version's divided by zero. They'd have to
write a loop to calculate the MLE version of variance.

I see the same benefit in having both MLE and
unbiased versions of sample variance calcs as
having multiple parameterizations.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
parts:
Oh, ok. For the variance() function in Stan we should divide by n-1. That is standard. If you'd like it to also operate when n=1, the function could simply be defined as 0 when n=1. (In R, var() returns NA when n=1, but I have no problem with variance() returning 0). Then if you want the other thing, you can just compute variance*(n-1)/n and everybody will be happy.

I don't have a strong feeling about the ESS thing because I never run just one chain. For now, I'm happy either working with the split chains or else having an "if" statement so that when #chains is more than 1 it uses our formula, but when #chains=1, it splits first.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
parts:
Andrew -- make sure you get to the last item and
understand how integer arithmetic works in Stan and C++
(and Java and Python and every other language I know other
than BUGS, R and MATLAB).

On 8/29/12 5:55 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

> I don't have a strong feeling about the ESS thing because I never run just one chain.
> For now, I'm happy either working with the split chains or else having an "if"
> statement so that when #chains is more than 1 it uses our formula, but when #chains=1, it splits first.

No problem. We can change the definition.

First, I'll work through the math to make sure it works.
It seems to me like we'll just be jacking up the variance
by a fixed factor (offhand, I'm guessing 1/4) this way, but
I'll verify.

Then it requires changing not only the code, but also the Stan doc,
the RStan doc, and the Stan unit tests. So when I or someone
else has an hour or two, we can make the changes.
> Oh, ok. For the variance() function in Stan we should divide by n-1. That is standard.

It certainly matches BUGS, R and MATLAB, which is why
I coded it that way in the first place.

> If you'd like it to also operate when n=1, the function could simply be defined as 0 when n=1.
> (In R, var() returns NA when n=1, but I have no problem with variance() returning 0).

I'd rather throw an error. If we return anything,
it should be +infinity. Returning 0 seems like a recipe
for errors.
> Then if you want the other thing, you can just compute variance*(n-1)/n and everybody will be happy.

But a special variance_mle() function would do it more
efficiently and in a way less prone to errors.

For example, the astute reader of the Stan doc would realize
that

(n-1) / n * variance = 0

if n is an integer, because Stan follows C++ in evaluating
arithmetic expressions, which means (a) it's left associative,
making this equal to:

((n-1) / n) * variance

and (b) uses integer arithmetic for integers, which rounds
fractions down, so that (n-1)/n = 0.

This should probably go into the Stan-for-BUGS-users section.

Having said all this, Guido von Rossum, developer of Python,
regrets his choice to implement integer division following
C conventions:

http://python-history.blogspot.com/2009/03/problem-with-integer-division.html

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ess for one chain
parts: I do not want to have a variance_mle() function. The sample variance is defined as dividing by n-1. If n=0, the result is not infinity, it's 0/0. I really don't see a problem with defining it to be 0 when n=1. In any situation I can think of where we would be calculating var() and happen to have n=1, I don't think of it as an error, really.
